# wallee - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wallee/0.2.7/wallee/

## Expand description

This library provides [ wallee::Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error
type for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

This crate is a fork of [ anyhow](https://github.com/dtolnay/anyhow) with support for
caller location tracking. This is useful when debug information is not included in the build.
The caller location attached to

[includes the file, line and column where the error originated.](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)

`wallee::Error`[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Use `Result<T, wallee::Error>`, or equivalently`wallee::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error`trait.`use wallee::Result; fn get_cluster_info() -> Result<ClusterMap> { let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?; let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?; Ok(map) }`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like “No such file or directory” can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use wallee::{Context, Result}; fn main() -> Result<()> { ... it.detach().context("Failed to detach the important thing")?; let content = std::fs::read(path) .with_context(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path))?; ... }``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() { Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)), None => Err(error), }`
-
A backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Wallee works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use thiserror::Error; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum FormatError { #[error("Invalid header (expected {expected:?}, got {found:?})")] InvalidHeader { expected: String, found: String, }, #[error("Missing attribute: {0}")] MissingAttribute(String), }`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `wallee!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces a`wallee::Error`.`return Err(wallee!("Missing attribute: {}", missing));`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!("Missing attribute: {}", missing);`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wallee](https://docs.rs/macro.wallee.html)as format_err;

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bail](https://docs.rs/macro.bail.html)
- Return early with an error.
- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Return early with an error if a condition is not satisfied.
- [wallee](https://docs.rs/macro.wallee.html)
- Construct an ad-hoc error from a string or existing non-`wallee`error value.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# sentry_options_validation - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sentry-options-validation/1.2.0/sentry_options_validation/

## Expand description

Schema validation library for sentry-options.

Schemas are loaded once into a [ SchemaRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaRegistry.html) and shared via

`Arc`.
Values are validated against schemas as complete objects.Values refresh lazily on read on the same thread. A read past
the staleness window re-reads the values directory on the calling thread
and publishes the new snapshot via `ArcSwap` (last-writer-wins). The full
scheme is in `docs/architecture.md`; the memory-ordering invariants are
documented inline in the `refresh` method below.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Namespace](https://docs.rs/struct.NamespaceSchema.html)- Schema
- Schema for a namespace, containing validator and option metadata
- [Option](https://docs.rs/struct.OptionMetadata.html)- Metadata
- Metadata for a single option in a namespace schema
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for loading and storing schemas
- [Values](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesStore.html)- Store
- Validates and serves option values, reloading them lazily on read and
serving the current snapshot lock-free via `ArcSwap`. See`refresh`for the staleness window and memory-ordering details.

- Errors that can occur during schema and value validation

- Environment variable to suppress missing directory errors
- [PRODUCTION_](https://docs.rs/constant.PRODUCTION_OPTIONS_DIR.html)- OPTIONS_ - DIR

- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_k8s_name_component.html)- k8s_ - name_ - component

# wmill - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wmill/1.746.0/wmill/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#windmill-rust-sdk)Windmill Rust SDK

A Rust client library for interacting with [Windmill](https://www.windmill.dev/) API, providing type-safe abstractions for variables, resources, scripts, jobs, and state management.

[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
wmill = "0.1.0"
```
For async support (recommended):

```
[dependencies]
wmill = { version = "0.1.0", features = ["async"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#initialize-client)Initialize Client

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmill::Windmill;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Read config from env vars
    let wm = Windmill::default()?;

    // Or override specific values
    let wm = Windmill::new(
        Some("custom_token".to_string()),
        Some("my_workspace".to_string()),
        Some("http://localhost:8000".to_string())
    )?;

    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#variables)Variables

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Get variable (auto-parsed)
let db_config: serde_json::Value = wm.get_variable("u/admin/db_config").await?;
// Get raw variable
let raw_text = wm.get_variable_raw("u/user/text_note").await?;
// Set variable
wm.set_variable("new_value".to_string(), "u/user/my_var", false).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#resources)Resources

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Get resource (typed)
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct DbConfig { host: String, port: u16 }
let config: DbConfig = wm.get_resource("u/admin/db").await?;
// Get raw resource
let raw_json = wm.get_resource_any("u/admin/db").await?;
// Set resource
wm.set_resource(
    Some(serde_json::json!({"host": "localhost", "port": 5432})),
    "u/admin/db",
    "postgresql"
).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#scripts)Scripts

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Run script async
let job_id = wm.run_script_async(
    "u/user/my_script",
    false,
    serde_json::json!({"param": "value"}),
    Some(10) // Schedule in 10 seconds
).await?;
// Run script sync
let result = wm.run_script_sync(
    "u/user/my_script",
    false,
    serde_json::json!({"param": "value"}),
    Some(10),
    Some(30), // 30s timeout
    true,     // Verbose
    true      // Assert result not None
).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#jobs)Jobs

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Wait for job completion
let result = wm.wait_job(&job_id, Some(60), true, true).await?;
// Get job status
let status = wm.get_job_status(&job_id).await?; // Running/Waiting/Completed
// Get result directly
let result = wm.get_result(&job_id).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#state-management)State Management

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Get typed state
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct ScriptState { counter: i32 }
let state: ScriptState = wm.get_state().await?;
// Get raw state
let raw_state = wm.get_state_any().await?;
// Update state
wm.set_state(Some(serde_json::json!({"counter": 42}))).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#progress-tracking)Progress Tracking

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Set job progress
wm.set_progress(75, None).await?; // Uses current job ID from env
// Get job progress
let progress = wm.get_progress(Some(job_id.to_string())).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-api-calls)Custom API Calls

The SDK provides direct access to underlying API endpoints through the `call_api` method, which works in both async and sync contexts:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Async usage
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let wm = Windmill::default()?;

    // Make direct API call to get user
    let user = wm.call_api(wmill::apis::admin_api::get_user(
        &wm.client_config,
        &wm.workspace,
        "Alice"
    )).await;

    println!("User details: {:?}", user);
    Ok(())
}
// Sync usage
fn main() {
    let wm = Windmill::default().unwrap();

    // Make direct API call to get user
    let user = wm.call_api(wmill::apis::admin_api::get_user(
        &wm.client_config,
        &wm.workspace,
        "Bob"
    ));

    println!("User details: {:?}", user);
}
```
This advanced feature allows access to any Windmill API endpoint, even those not covered by the SDK’s convenience methods. Use this when:

- Need to access newer/undocumented API endpoints
- Require fine-grained control over API requests
- Existing abstractions don’t meet specific needs

[§](https://docs.rs#environment-variables)Environment Variables

The SDK uses these environment variables:

| Variable | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `WM_TOKEN` | ✅ | Authentication token |
| `WM_WORKSPACE` | ✅ | Workspace name |
| `BASE_INTERNAL_URL` | ✅ | API base URL (without `/api`) |
| `WM_JOB_ID` | Optional | Current job ID for progress tracking |
| `WM_STATE_PATH_NEW` | Optional | State path override |

# wayland_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-cursor/0.31.14/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/wayland_cursor/

## Expand description

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to re-implement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a [ CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html), which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the [ get_cursor()](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.get_cursor) method, you can load a
specific

[, which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to attach them to a wayland surface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
// Load the default cursor theme.
let mut cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(&connection, shm, 32)
    .expect("Could not load cursor theme");
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait")
    .expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
    // Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
    let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
    let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
    // Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
    let buffer = &cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
    // and attach it to a wl_surface.
    cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
    cursor_surface.commit();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(fr_info.frame_duration as u64));
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)
- A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorImageBuffer.html)- Image - Buffer
- A buffer containing a cursor image.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)- Theme
- Represents a cursor theme loaded from the system.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameAndDuration.html)- AndDuration
- Which frame to show, and for how long.

[109](https://docs.rs#109)    /// Load a cursor theme from system defaults.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    ///
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    /// Same as calling the following:
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    /// ```
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    /// # use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// # use wayland_client::{Connection, backend::InvalidId, protocol::wl_shm};
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    /// # fn example(conn: &Connection, shm: wl_shm::WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<CursorTheme, InvalidId> {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// CursorTheme::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    /// # }
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// ```
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    pub fn load(conn: &Connection, shm: WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)        Self::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    }
[122](https://docs.rs#122)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// Load a cursor theme, using `name` as fallback.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    ///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// The theme name and cursor size are read from the `XCURSOR_THEME` and
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// `XCURSOR_SIZE` environment variables, respectively, or from the provided variables
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// if those are invalid.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    pub fn load_or(
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        conn: &Connection,
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        shm: WlShm,
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        name: &str,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)        mut size: u32,
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    ) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        let name_string = String::from(name);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)        let name = &env::var("XCURSOR_THEME").unwrap_or(name_string);
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        if let Ok(var) = env::var("XCURSOR_SIZE") {
[138](https://docs.rs#138)            if let Ok(int) = var.parse() {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)                size = int;
[140](https://docs.rs#140)            }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)        Self::load_from_name(conn, shm, name, size)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    }
[145](https://docs.rs#145)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// Create a new cursor theme, ignoring the system defaults.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    pub fn load_from_name(
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        conn: &Connection,
[149](https://docs.rs#149)        shm: WlShm,
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        name: &str,
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        size: u32,
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    ) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> {
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        // Set some minimal cursor size to hold it. We're not using `size` argument for that,
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        // because the actual size that we'll use depends on theme sizes available on a system.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        // The minimal size covers most common minimal theme size, which is 16.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        const INITIAL_POOL_SIZE: i32 = 16 * 16 * 4;
[157](https://docs.rs#157)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        //  Create shm.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        let mem_fd = create_shm_fd().expect("Shm fd allocation failed");
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        let mut file = File::from(mem_fd);
[161](https://docs.rs#161)        file.set_len(INITIAL_POOL_SIZE as u64).expect("Failed to set buffer length");
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        // Ensure that we have the same we requested.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        file.write_all(&[0; INITIAL_POOL_SIZE as usize]).expect("Write to shm fd failed");
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        // Flush to ensure the compositor has access to the buffer when it tries to map it.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        file.flush().expect("Flush on shm fd failed");
[167](https://docs.rs#167)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)        let pool_id = conn.send_request(
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            &shm,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)            wl_shm::Request::CreatePool { fd: file.as_fd(), size: INITIAL_POOL_SIZE },
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            Some(Arc::new(IgnoreObjectData)),
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        )?;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        let pool = WlShmPool::from_id(conn, pool_id)?;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        let name = String::from(name);
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        Ok(Self {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            name,
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            file,
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            size,
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            pool,
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            pool_size: INITIAL_POOL_SIZE,
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            cursors: Vec::new(),
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            backend: conn.backend().downgrade(),
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            fallback: None,
[186](https://docs.rs#186)        })
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    /// Retrieve a cursor from the theme.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// This method returns [`None`] if this cursor is not provided either by the theme, or by one of its parents.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    ///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// If a [fallback is set], it will use the data returned by the fallback.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    ///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// [fallback is set]: Self::set_fallback()
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    pub fn get_cursor(&mut self, name: &str) -> Option<&Cursor> {
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        match self.cursors.iter().position(|cursor| cursor.name == name) {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)            Some(i) => Some(&self.cursors[i]),
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            None => {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)                let cursor = match self.load_cursor(name, self.size) {
[201](https://docs.rs#201)                    None => {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)                        let fallback = self.fallback.as_ref()?;
[203](https://docs.rs#203)                        let data = fallback.0(name, self.size)?;
[204](https://docs.rs#204)                        let images = xparser::parse_xcursor(&data)?;
[205](https://docs.rs#205)                        let conn = Connection::from_backend(self.backend.upgrade()?);
[206](https://docs.rs#206)                        Cursor::new(&conn, name, self, &images, self.size)
[207](https://docs.rs#207)                    }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)                    Some(cursor) => cursor,
[209](https://docs.rs#209)                };
[210](https://docs.rs#210)                self.cursors.push(cursor);
[211](https://docs.rs#211)                self.cursors.iter().last()
[212](https://docs.rs#212)            }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// Set a fallback to load the cursor data, in case the system theme is missing a cursor that you need.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    ///
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// Your fallback will be invoked with the name and size of the requested cursor and should return a byte
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// array with the contents of an `xcursor` file, or [`None`] if you don't provide a fallback for this cursor.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// For example, this defines a generic fallback cursor image and uses it for all missing cursors:
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    /// ```ignore
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// use wayland_client::{Connection, backend::InvalidId, protocol::wl_shm};
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// fn example(conn: &Connection, shm: wl_shm::WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<CursorTheme, InvalidId> {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    ///   let mut theme = CursorTheme::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)?;
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    ///   theme.set_fallback(|name, size| {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    ///       include_bytes!("./icons/default")
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///   });
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    ///   Ok(theme)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// ```
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    pub fn set_fallback<F>(&mut self, fallback: F)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    where
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        F: Fn(&str, u32) -> Option<Cow<'static, [u8]>> + Send + Sync + 'static,
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        self.fallback = Some(FallBack::new(fallback))
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// This function loads a cursor, parses it and pushes the images onto the shm pool.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    ///
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// Keep in mind that if the cursor is already loaded, the function will make a duplicate.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    fn load_cursor(&mut self, name: &str, size: u32) -> Option<Cursor> {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        let conn = Connection::from_backend(self.backend.upgrade()?);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        let icon_path = XCursorTheme::load(&self.name).load_icon(name)?;
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        let mut icon_file = File::open(icon_path).ok()?;
[247](https://docs.rs#247)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let mut buf = Vec::new();
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        let images = {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            icon_file.read_to_end(&mut buf).ok()?;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)            xparser::parse_xcursor(&buf)?
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        };
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        Some(Cursor::new(&conn, name, self, &images, size))
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    }
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// Grow the wl_shm_pool this theme is stored on.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// This method does nothing if the provided size is smaller or equal to the pool's current size.
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    fn grow(&mut self, size: i32) {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        if size > self.pool_size {
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            self.file.set_len(size as u64).expect("Failed to set new buffer length");
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            self.pool.resize(size);
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            self.pool_size = size;
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    }

[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[271](https://docs.rs#271)pub struct Cursor {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    name: String,
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    images: Vec<CursorImageBuffer>,
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    total_duration: u32,
[275](https://docs.rs#275)}
[276](https://docs.rs#276)
[277](https://docs.rs#277)impl Cursor {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// Construct a new Cursor.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    /// Each of the provided images will be written into `theme`.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// This will also grow `theme.pool` if necessary.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    fn new(
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        conn: &Connection,
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        name: &str,
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        theme: &mut CursorTheme,
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        images: &[XCursorImage],
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        size: u32,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    ) -> Self {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)        let mut total_duration = 0;
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        let images: Vec<CursorImageBuffer> = Self::nearest_images(size, images)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            .map(|image| {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)                let buffer = CursorImageBuffer::new(conn, theme, image);
[293](https://docs.rs#293)                total_duration += buffer.delay;
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)                buffer
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            })
[297](https://docs.rs#297)            .collect();
[298](https://docs.rs#298)
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        Self { total_duration, name: String::from(name), images }
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    fn nearest_images(size: u32, images: &[XCursorImage]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &XCursorImage> {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        // Follow the nominal size of the cursor to choose the nearest
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        let nearest_image =
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            images.iter().min_by_key(|image| (size as i32 - image.size as i32).abs()).unwrap();
[306](https://docs.rs#306)
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        images.iter().filter(move |image| {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            image.width == nearest_image.width && image.height == nearest_image.height
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        })
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    }
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// Given a time, calculate which frame to show, and how much time remains until the next frame.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    ///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// Time will wrap, so if for instance the cursor has an animation lasting 100ms,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// then calling this function with 5ms and 105ms as input gives the same output.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    pub fn frame_and_duration(&self, mut millis: u32) -> FrameAndDuration {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        millis %= self.total_duration;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        let mut res = 0;
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        for (i, img) in self.images.iter().enumerate() {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            if millis < img.delay {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                res = i;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                break;
[324](https://docs.rs#324)            }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            millis -= img.delay;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        }
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        FrameAndDuration { frame_index: res, frame_duration: millis }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    }
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    /// Total number of images forming this cursor animation
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    pub fn image_count(&self) -> usize {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        self.images.len()
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    }

[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// A buffer containing a cursor image.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// You can access the `WlBuffer` via `Deref`.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// Note that this buffer is internally managed by wayland-cursor, as such you should
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// not try to act on it beyond assigning it to `wl_surface`s.
[351](https://docs.rs#351)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[352](https://docs.rs#352)pub struct CursorImageBuffer {
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    buffer: WlBuffer,
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    delay: u32,
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    xhot: u32,
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    yhot: u32,
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    width: u32,
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    height: u32,
[359](https://docs.rs#359)}
[360](https://docs.rs#360)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)impl CursorImageBuffer {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// Construct a new CursorImageBuffer
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    ///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// This function appends the pixels of the image to the provided file,
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// and constructs a wl_buffer on that data.
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    fn new(conn: &Connection, theme: &mut CursorTheme, image: &XCursorImage) -> Self {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        let buf = &image.pixels_rgba;
[368](https://docs.rs#368)        let offset = theme.file.seek(SeekFrom::End(0)).unwrap();
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        // Resize memory before writing to it to handle shm correctly.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        let new_size = offset + buf.len() as u64;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        theme.grow(new_size as i32);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        theme.file.write_all(buf).unwrap();
[375](https://docs.rs#375)
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        let buffer_id = conn
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            .send_request(
[378](https://docs.rs#378)                &theme.pool,
[379](https://docs.rs#379)                wl_shm_pool::Request::CreateBuffer {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)                    offset: offset as i32,
[381](https://docs.rs#381)                    width: image.width as i32,
[382](https://docs.rs#382)                    height: image.height as i32,
[383](https://docs.rs#383)                    stride: (image.width * 4) as i32,
[384](https://docs.rs#384)                    format: WEnum::Value(Format::Argb8888),
[385](https://docs.rs#385)                },
[386](https://docs.rs#386)                Some(Arc::new(IgnoreObjectData)),
[387](https://docs.rs#387)            )
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            .unwrap();
[389](https://docs.rs#389)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        let buffer = WlBuffer::from_id(conn, buffer_id).unwrap();
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        Self {
[393](https://docs.rs#393)            buffer,
[394](https://docs.rs#394)            delay: image.delay,
[395](https://docs.rs#395)            xhot: image.xhot,
[396](https://docs.rs#396)            yhot: image.yhot,
[397](https://docs.rs#397)            width: image.width,
[398](https://docs.rs#398)            height: image.height,
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)

[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// Which frame to show, and for how long.

[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// Create a shared file descriptor in memory.
[438](https://docs.rs#438)fn create_shm_fd() -> IoResult<OwnedFd> {
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    // Only try memfd on systems that provide it, (like Linux, Android)
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    #[cfg(any(target_os = "linux", target_os = "android"))]
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    loop {
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        match memfd_create(
[443](https://docs.rs#443)            CStr::from_bytes_with_nul(b"wayland-cursor-rs\0").unwrap(),
[444](https://docs.rs#444)            MemfdFlags::CLOEXEC,
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        ) {
[446](https://docs.rs#446)            Ok(fd) => return Ok(fd),
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            Err(Errno::INTR) => continue,
[448](https://docs.rs#448)            Err(Errno::NOSYS) => break,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)            Err(errno) => return Err(errno.into()),
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        }
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    }
[452](https://docs.rs#452)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    // Fallback to using shm_open.
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    let sys_time = SystemTime::now();
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    let mut mem_file_handle = format!(
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        "/wayland-cursor-rs-{}",
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        sys_time.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().subsec_nanos()
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    );
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    loop {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        match shm::open(
[461](https://docs.rs#461)            mem_file_handle.as_str(),
[462](https://docs.rs#462)            shm::OFlags::CREATE | shm::OFlags::EXCL | shm::OFlags::RDWR,
[463](https://docs.rs#463)            Mode::RUSR | Mode::WUSR,
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        ) {
[465](https://docs.rs#465)            Ok(fd) => match shm::unlink(mem_file_handle.as_str()) {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)                Ok(_) => return Ok(fd),
[467](https://docs.rs#467)                Err(errno) => return Err(IoError::from(errno)),
[468](https://docs.rs#468)            },
[469](https://docs.rs#469)            Err(Errno::EXIST) => {
[470](https://docs.rs#470)                // If a file with that handle exists then change the handle
[471](https://docs.rs#471)                mem_file_handle = format!(
[472](https://docs.rs#472)                    "/wayland-cursor-rs-{}",
[473](https://docs.rs#473)                    sys_time.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().subsec_nanos()
[474](https://docs.rs#474)                );
[475](https://docs.rs#475)                continue;
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)            Err(Errno::INTR) => continue,
[478](https://docs.rs#478)            Err(errno) => return Err(IoError::from(errno)),
[479](https://docs.rs#479)        }
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    }
[481](https://docs.rs#481)}
[482](https://docs.rs#482)

Retrieve a cursor from the theme.

This method returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if this cursor is not provided either by the theme, or by one of its parents.

If a [fallback is set](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.set_fallback), it will use the data returned by the fallback.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_cursor/lib.rs.html#233-238)#### pub fn [set_fallback](https://docs.rs#method.set_fallback)<F>(&mut self, fallback: F)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_cursor/lib.rs.html#233-238)

#### pub fn [set_fallback](https://docs.rs#method.set_fallback)<F>(&mut self, fallback: F)

Set a fallback to load the cursor data, in case the system theme is missing a cursor that you need.

Your fallback will be invoked with the name and size of the requested cursor and should return a byte
array with the contents of an `xcursor` file, or [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if you don’t provide a fallback for this cursor.

For example, this defines a generic fallback cursor image and uses it for all missing cursors:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
use wayland_client::{Connection, backend::InvalidId, protocol::wl_shm};
fn example(conn: &Connection, shm: wl_shm::WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<CursorTheme, InvalidId> {
  let mut theme = CursorTheme::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)?;
  theme.set_fallback(|name, size| {
      include_bytes!("./icons/default")
  });
  Ok(theme)
}
```

Given a time, calculate which frame to show, and how much time remains until the next frame.

Time will wrap, so if for instance the cursor has an animation lasting 100ms, then calling this function with 5ms and 105ms as input gives the same output.

# wayland_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-cursor/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/wayland_cursor/

## Expand description

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to re-implement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a [ CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html), which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the [ get_cursor()](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.get_cursor) method, you can load a
specific

[, which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to attach them to a wayland surface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
// Load the default cursor theme.
let mut cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(&connection, shm, 32)
    .expect("Could not load cursor theme");
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait")
    .expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
    // Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
    let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
    let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
    // Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
    let buffer = &cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
    // and attach it to a wl_surface.
    cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
    cursor_surface.commit();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(fr_info.frame_duration as u64));
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)
- A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorImageBuffer.html)- Image - Buffer
- A buffer containing a cursor image.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)- Theme
- Represents a cursor theme loaded from the system.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameAndDuration.html)- AndDuration
- Which frame to show, and for how long.

# wayland_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-cursor/latest/wayland_cursor/

## Expand description

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to re-implement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a [ CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html), which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the [ get_cursor()](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.get_cursor) method, you can load a
specific

[, which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to attach them to a wayland surface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
// Load the default cursor theme.
let mut cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(&connection, shm, 32)
    .expect("Could not load cursor theme");
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait")
    .expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
    // Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
    let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
    let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
    // Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
    let buffer = &cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
    // and attach it to a wl_surface.
    cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
    cursor_surface.commit();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(fr_info.frame_duration as u64));
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)
- A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorImageBuffer.html)- Image - Buffer
- A buffer containing a cursor image.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)- Theme
- Represents a cursor theme loaded from the system.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameAndDuration.html)- AndDuration
- Which frame to show, and for how long.

# rustix 1.1.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/^1.0.2

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends. It
uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports [Windows Sockets 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/windows-sockets-start-page-2)
(Winsock), the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and
more portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature, or
set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/buffer/index.html)

`rustix::buffer`[,](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API modules are conditional with cargo feature flags.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/ioctl.html)

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

## Similar crates

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/simple_libc)

`simple_libc`[,](https://crates.io/crates/unix)

`unix`[,](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi`[.](https://lib.rs/crates/rusl)

`rusl``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`OwnedFd`[to manipulate file descriptors rather than](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/trait.AsFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,
`rustix` has an optimized and flexible filename argument mechanism that allows
users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the
[ sc](https://crates.io/crates/sc), and

[crates, using the Rust](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``asm!` macro. `rustix` can also
use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime` on all
architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s syscalls
report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `CWD` constant exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently [Rust 1.63](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2022/08/11/Rust-1.63.0.html). This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

## Minimum Linux Version

On Linux platforms, rustix requires at least Linux 3.2. This is at most the oldest Linux version supported by:

- [any current Rust target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/rustc/platform-support.html), or
- [kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/releases.html)at the time of rustix's- [MSRV](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)release. The specifics of this policy may change in the future, but we intend it to always reflect “very old” Linux versions.

# wayland-client 0.31.14 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-client/^0.31.14

# wayland-client

Client side API for the Wayland protocol. This crate provides infrastructure for manipulating
Wayland objects, as well as object definitions for the core Wayland protocol. Protocol extensions
can be supported as well by combining this crate with `wayland-protocols`, which provides object
definitions for a large set of extensions.

See the [crate-level documentation](https://docs.rs/wayland-client) for usage explanations.

**Note:** This crate is a low-level interface to the Wayland protocol. If you are looking for a more
battery-included toolkit for writing a Wayland client app, you may consider
[Smithay's Client Toolkit](https://crates.io/crates/smithay-client-toolkit), which is built on top
of it.

# wayland-cursor 0.26.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-cursor/0.26.5

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to reimplement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a `CursorTheme`,
which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the `get_cursor` method, you can load a specific `Cursor`,
which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the
means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at
what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to
attach them to a wayland surface.

# Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
# use std::thread::sleep;
# use std::time::{Instant, Duration};
let cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(32, wl_shm);
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait").expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
// Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
// Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
let buffer = cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
// and attach it to a wl_surface.
cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
cursor_surface.commit();
sleep(fr_info.frame_duration);
}
```

---

# wayland-cursor 0.25.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-cursor/0.25.0

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate contains bindings to the `libwayland-cursor.so` library.

These utilities allow you to load cursor images in order to match your cursors to the ones of the system.

First of all, the function `load_theme` will allow you to load a
`CursorTheme`, which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, you can load a specific `Cursor`, which can contain
several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the
means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at
what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to
attach them to a wayland surface.

---

# wayland_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-cursor

## Expand description

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to re-implement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a [ CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html), which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the [ get_cursor()](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.get_cursor) method, you can load a
specific

[, which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to attach them to a wayland surface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
// Load the default cursor theme.
let mut cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(&connection, shm, 32)
    .expect("Could not load cursor theme");
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait")
    .expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
    // Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
    let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
    let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
    // Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
    let buffer = &cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
    // and attach it to a wl_surface.
    cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
    cursor_surface.commit();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(fr_info.frame_duration as u64));
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)
- A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorImageBuffer.html)- Image - Buffer
- A buffer containing a cursor image.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)- Theme
- Represents a cursor theme loaded from the system.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameAndDuration.html)- AndDuration
- Which frame to show, and for how long.

# rustix 1.1.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/1.1.4

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends. It
uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports [Windows Sockets 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/windows-sockets-start-page-2)
(Winsock), the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and
more portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature, or
set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/buffer/index.html)

`rustix::buffer`[,](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API modules are conditional with cargo feature flags.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/ioctl.html)

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

## Similar crates

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/simple_libc)

`simple_libc`[,](https://crates.io/crates/unix)

`unix`[,](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi`[.](https://lib.rs/crates/rusl)

`rusl``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`OwnedFd`[to manipulate file descriptors rather than](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/trait.AsFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,
`rustix` has an optimized and flexible filename argument mechanism that allows
users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the
[ sc](https://crates.io/crates/sc), and

[crates, using the Rust](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``asm!` macro. `rustix` can also
use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime` on all
architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s syscalls
report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `CWD` constant exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently [Rust 1.63](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2022/08/11/Rust-1.63.0.html). This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

## Minimum Linux Version

On Linux platforms, rustix requires at least Linux 3.2. This is at most the oldest Linux version supported by:

- [any current Rust target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/rustc/platform-support.html), or
- [kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/releases.html)at the time of rustix's- [MSRV](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)release. The specifics of this policy may change in the future, but we intend it to always reflect “very old” Linux versions.

# bitflags - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bitflags/^2.4.0/

## Expand description

Generate types for C-style flags with ergonomic APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `bitflags` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.bitflags]
version = "2.13.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-flags-types)Generating flags types

Use the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro to generate flags types:

```
use bitflags::bitflags;
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
See the docs for the `bitflags` macro for the full syntax.

Also see the [ example_generated](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html) module for an example of what the

`bitflags` macro generates for a flags type.[§](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags)Externally defined flags

If you’re generating flags types for an external source, such as a C API, you can define
an extra unnamed flag as a mask of all bits the external source may ever set. Usually this would be all bits (`!0`):

```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
        // The source may set any bits
        const _ = !0;
    }
}
```
Why should you do this? Generated methods like `all` and truncating operators like `!` only consider
bits in defined flags. Adding an unnamed flag makes those methods consider additional bits,
without generating additional constants for them. It helps compatibility when the external source
may start setting additional bits at any time. The [known and unknown bits](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)
section has more details on this behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derives)Custom derives

You can derive some traits on generated flags types if you enable Cargo features. The following libraries are currently supported:

- `serde`: Support- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`, using text for human-readable formats, and a raw number for binary formats.
- `arbitrary`: Support- `#[derive(Arbitrary)]`, only generating flags values with known bits.
- `bytemuck`: Support- `#[derive(Pod, Zeroable)]`, for casting between flags values and their underlying bits values.

You can also define your own flags type outside of the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro and then use it to generate methods.
This can be useful if you need a custom

`#[derive]` attribute for a library that `bitflags` doesn’t
natively support:```
#[derive(SomeTrait)]
pub struct Flags(u32);
bitflags! {
    impl Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#adding-custom-methods)Adding custom methods

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro supports attributes on generated flags types within the macro itself, while

`impl` blocks can be added outside of it:```
bitflags! {
    // Attributes can be applied to flags types
    #[repr(transparent)]
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
// Impl blocks can be added to flags types
impl Flags {
    pub fn as_u64(&self) -> u64 {
        self.bits() as u64
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-flags)Renaming flags

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro recognizes a special

`#[bitflags(flag_name = "<value>")]` attribute on flags values to rename them:```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        // Add the attribute to a flag to change its name
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "a")]
        const A = 0b00000001;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "b")]
        const B = 0b00000010;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "c")]
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
When applied to a flag value, instead of using its identifier, like `A` as the name, it’ll use the given string. This
doesn’t affect the identifier of the constant itself, just the name recognized when parsing and formatting.

[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-flags-values)Working with flags values

Use generated constants and standard bitwise operators to interact with flags values:

```
// union
let ab = Flags::A | Flags::B;
// intersection
let a = ab & Flags::A;
// difference
let b = ab - Flags::A;
// complement
let c = !ab;
```
See the docs for the [ Flags](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html) trait for more details on operators and how they behave.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-and-parsing)Formatting and parsing

`bitflags` defines a text format that can be used to convert any flags value to and from strings.

See the [ parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html) module for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#specification)Specification

The terminology and behavior of generated flags types is
[specified in the source repository](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags/blob/main/spec.md).
Details are repeated in these docs where appropriate, but is exhaustively listed in the spec. Some
things are worth calling out explicitly here.

[§](https://docs.rs#flags-types-flags-values-flags)Flags types, flags values, flags

The spec and these docs use consistent terminology to refer to things in the bitflags domain:

- **Bits type**: A type that defines a fixed number of bits at specific locations.
- **Flag**: A set of bits in a bits type that may have a unique name.
- **Flags type**: A set of defined flags over a specific bits type.
- **Flags value**: An instance of a flags type using its specific bits value for storage.

```
bitflags! {
    struct FlagsType: u8 {
//                    -- Bits type
//         --------- Flags type
        const A = 1;
//            ----- Flag
    }
}
let flag = FlagsType::A;
//  ---- Flags value
```
[§](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)Known and unknown bits

Any bits in a flag you define are called *known bits*. Any other bits are *unknown bits*.
In the following flags type:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 << 1;
        const C = 1 << 2;
    }
}
```
The known bits are `0b0000_0111` and the unknown bits are `0b1111_1000`.

`bitflags` doesn’t guarantee that a flags value will only ever have known bits set, but some operators
will unset any unknown bits they encounter. In a future version of `bitflags`, all operators will
unset unknown bits.

If you’re using `bitflags` for flags types defined externally, such as from C, you probably want all
bits to be considered known, in case that external source changes. You can do this using an unnamed
flag, as described in [externally defined flags](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-bit-flags)Zero-bit flags

Flags with no bits set should be avoided because they interact strangely with [ Flags::contains](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.contains)
and

[. A zero-bit flag is always contained, but is never intersected. The names of zero-bit flags can be parsed, but are never formatted.](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.intersects)

`Flags::intersects`[§](https://docs.rs#multi-bit-flags)Multi-bit flags

Flags that set multiple bits should be avoided unless each bit is also in a single-bit flag. Take the following flags type as an example:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 | 1 << 1;
    }
}
```
The result of `Flags::A ^ Flags::B` is `0b0000_0010`, which doesn’t correspond to either
`Flags::A` or `Flags::B` even though it’s still a known bit.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [example_](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html)- generated
- This module shows an example of code generated by the macro. **IT MUST NOT BE USED OUTSIDE THIS CRATE**.
- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- Yield the bits of a source flags value in a set of contained flags values.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Parsing flags from text.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html)
- Generate a flags type.
- [bitflags_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags_match.html)- match
- A macro that matches flags values, similar to Rust’s `match`statement.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Flag](https://docs.rs/struct.Flag.html)
- A defined flags value that may be named or unnamed.

# flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/^1.0/

## Expand description

A DEFLATE-based stream compression/decompression library

This library provides support for compression and decompression of DEFLATE-based streams:

- the DEFLATE format itself
- the zlib format
- gzip

These three formats are all closely related and largely only differ in their headers/footers. This crate has three types in each submodule for dealing with these three formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

In addition to supporting three formats, this crate supports several different
backends, controlled through this crate’s *features flags*:

-
`default`, or`rust_backend`- this implementation currently uses the`miniz_oxide`crate which is a port of`miniz.c`to Rust. This feature does not require a C compiler, and only uses safe Rust code.Note that the `rust_backend`feature may at some point be switched to use`zlib-rs`, and that`miniz_oxide`should be used explicitly if this is not desired.
-
`zlib-rs`- this implementation utilizes the`zlib-rs`crate, a Rust rewrite of zlib. This backend is the fastest, at the cost of some`unsafe`Rust code.

Several backends implemented in C are also available. These are useful in case you are already using a specific C implementation and need the result of compression to be bit-identical. See the crate’s README for details on the available C backends.

The `zlib-rs` backend typically outperforms all the C implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `miniz_oxide`- *(enabled by default)*— This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.
- `default`

[§](https://docs.rs#user-facing-backend-features)User-Facing Backend Features

Choose one of these features to select the compression backend.
Only one backend should be enabled at a time, or else one will see an unstable order which is currently
`zlib-ng`, `zlib-rs`, `cloudflare_zlib`, `miniz_oxide` and which may change at any time.

-
`rust_backend`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend (default). This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.Note that this feature at some point may be switched to use `zlib-rs`instead.
-
`zlib-rs``unsafe`code. It does not require a C compiler but uses`unsafe`Rust for optimization.
-
`miniz_oxide`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend.
-
`zlib`
-
`zlib-default``zlib`but enables additional features from libz-sys.
-
`zlib-ng-compat``zlib-ng`feature. When using this feature, if any crate in your dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly without`default-features = false`, you’ll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng. See[the libz-sys README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md)for details. To avoid that, use the`"zlib-ng"`feature instead.
-
`zlib-ng`
-
`cloudflare_zlib`- ⚠ Does not support 32-bit CPUs and is incompatible with mingw.
- ⚠ May cause conflicts if other crates use different zlib versions.

-
`miniz-sys``rust_backend`, provided for backwards compatibility. Use`rust_backend`instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#internal-features)Internal Features

These features are used internally for backend selection and should not be enabled directly by users. They are documented here to aid with maintenance.

- `any_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any zlib-based C backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib-rs`,- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_c_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any C based fully zlib compatible backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_impl`- *(enabled by default)*—- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any compression backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by all backend features to ensure at least one implementation is available. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#ambiguous-feature-selection)Ambiguous feature selection

As Cargo features are additive, while backends are not, there is an order in which backends become active if multiple are selected.

- zlib-ng
- zlib-rs
- cloudflare_zlib
- miniz_oxide

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

This crate consists of three main modules: `bufread`, `read`, and `write`. Each module
implements DEFLATE, zlib, and gzip for [ std::io::BufRead](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.BufRead.html) input types,

[input types, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`std::io::Read`[output types respectively.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write`Use the [ bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html) implementations if you can provide a

`BufRead` type for the input.
The `&[u8]` slice type implements the `BufRead` trait.The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) implementations conveniently wrap a

`Read` type in a `BufRead` implementation.
However, the `read` implementations may
[read past the end of the input data](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs/issues/338), making the

`Read` type useless for subsequent reads of the input. If you need to re-use the
`Read` type, wrap it in a [, use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/buffered/bufreader/struct.BufReader.html)

`std::io::BufReader``bufread` implementations,
and perform subsequent reads on the `BufReader`.The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) implementations are most useful when there is no way to create a

`BufRead`
type, notably when reading async iterators (streams).```
use futures::{Stream, StreamExt};
use std::io::{Result, Write as _};
async fn decompress_gzip_stream<S, I>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = I>,
    I: AsRef<[u8]>
{
    let mut stream = std::pin::pin!(stream);
    let mut w = Vec::<u8>::new();
    let mut decoder = flate2::write::GzDecoder::new(w);
    while let Some(input) = stream.next().await {
        decoder.write_all(input.as_ref())?;
    }
    decoder.finish()
}
```
Note that types which operate over a specific trait often implement the mirroring trait as well.
For example a `bufread::DeflateDecoder<T>` *also* implements the
[ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html) trait if

`T: Write`. That is, the “dual trait” is forwarded directly
to the underlying object if available.[§](https://docs.rs#about-multi-member-gzip-files)About multi-member Gzip files

While most `gzip` files one encounters will have a single *member* that can be read
with the [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html), there may be some files which have multiple members.

A [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html) will only read the first member of gzip data, which may unexpectedly
provide partial results when a multi-member gzip file is encountered.

`GzDecoder` is appropriate
for data that is designed to be read as single members from a multi-member file. `bufread::GzDecoder`
and `write::GzDecoder` also allow non-gzip data following gzip data to be handled.The [ MultiGzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html) on the other hand will decode all members of a

`gzip` file
into one consecutive stream of bytes, which hides the underlying *members*entirely. If a file contains non-gzip data after the gzip data, MultiGzDecoder will emit an error after decoding the gzip data. This behavior matches the

`gzip`,
`gunzip`, and `zcat` command line tools.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html)
- Types which operate over `BufRead`
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Read`
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Write`

# errno - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/errno/^0.3.10/

## Expand description

Cross-platform interface to the `errno` variable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use errno::{Errno, errno, set_errno};
// Get the current value of errno
let e = errno();
// Set the current value of errno
set_errno(e);
// Extract the error code as an i32
let code = e.0;
// Display a human-friendly error message
println!("Error {}: {}", code, e);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Errno](https://docs.rs/struct.Errno.html)
- Wraps a platform-specific error code.

---

# memoffset - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/memoffset/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

A crate used for calculating offsets of struct members and their spans.

This functionality currently can not be used in compile time code such as `const` or `const fn` definitions.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use memoffset::{offset_of, span_of};
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory {
    help_me_before_they_: [u8; 15],
    a: u32
}
assert_eq!(offset_of!(HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory, a), 15);
assert_eq!(span_of!(HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory, a), 15..19);
assert_eq!(span_of!(HelpMeIAmTrappedInAStructFactory, help_me_before_they_ .. a), 0..15);
```
This functionality can be useful, for example, for checksum calculations:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct Message {
    header: MessageHeader,
    fragment_index: u32,
    fragment_count: u32,
    payload: [u8; 1024],
    checksum: u16
}
let checksum_range = &raw[span_of!(Message, header..checksum)];
let checksum = crc16(checksum_range);
```

# serial_test - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serial_test/^2.0.0/

## Expand description

`serial_test` allows for the creation of serialised Rust tests using the [serial](https://docs.rs/attr.serial.html) attribute
e.g.

```
#[test]
#[serial]
fn test_serial_one() {
  // Do things
}
#[test]
#[serial]
fn test_serial_another() {
  // Do things
}
#[test]
#[parallel]
fn test_parallel_another() {
  // Do parallel things
}
```
Multiple tests with the [serial](https://docs.rs/attr.serial.html) attribute are guaranteed to be executed in serial. Ordering
of the tests is not guaranteed however. Other tests with the [parallel](https://docs.rs/attr.parallel.html) attribute may run
at the same time as each other, but not at the same time as a test with [serial](https://docs.rs/attr.serial.html). Tests with
neither attribute may run at any time and no guarantees are made about their timing!

For cases like doctests and integration tests where the tests are run as separate processes, we also support
[file_serial](https://docs.rs/attr.file_serial.html)/[file_parallel](https://docs.rs/attr.file_parallel.html), with similar properties but based off file locking. Note that there are no
guarantees about one test with [serial](https://docs.rs/attr.serial.html)/[parallel](https://docs.rs/attr.parallel.html) and another with [file_serial](https://docs.rs/attr.file_serial.html)/[file_parallel](https://docs.rs/attr.file_parallel.html)
as they lock using different methods.

```
#[test]
#[file_serial]
fn test_serial_three() {
  // Do things
}
```
-
`logging`*(enabled by default)*— Switches on debug logging (and requires the`log`package)
-
`async`*(enabled by default)*— Enables async features (and requires the`futures`package)
-
`file_locks``file_serial`/`file_parallel`macros (and requires the`fslock`package)

- Allows for the creation of file-serialised parallel Rust tests that won’t clash with file-serialised serial tests
- Allows for the creation of file-serialised Rust tests
- Allows for the creation of parallel Rust tests that won’t clash with serial tests
- Allows for the creation of serialised Rust tests
