# wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-client/0.31.14/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/wayland_client/

## Expand description

Interface for interacting with the Wayland protocol, client-side.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-concepts)General concepts

This crate is structured around four main objects: the [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) and

[structs, proxies (objects implementing the](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[trait), and the](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html)

`Proxy`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`The [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) is the heart of this crate. It represents your connection to the Wayland server, and
you’ll generally initialize it using the

[method, which will attempt to open a Wayland connection following the configuration specified by the ! environment.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.connect_to_env)

`Connection::connect_to_env()`Once you have a [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html), you can create an

[from it. This](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[will take care of processing events from the Wayland server and delivering them to your processing logic, in the form of a state struct with several](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[implementations (see below).](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`Each of the Wayland objects you can manipulate is represented by a struct implementing the [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html)
trait. Those structs are automatically generated from the wayland XML protocol specification. This crate
provides the types generated from the core protocol in the

[module. For other standard protocols, see the](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol``wayland-protocols` crate.[§](https://docs.rs#event-dispatching)Event dispatching

The core event dispatching logic provided by this crate is built around the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) struct. In
this paradigm, receiving and processing events is a two-step process:

- First, events are read from the Wayland socket. For each event, the backend figures out which `EventQueue`
- Then, the `EventQueue``Dispatch::event()``State`value that was provided to it.

The main goal of this structure is to make your `State` accessible without synchronization to most of
your event-processing logic, to reduce the plumbing costs. See [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)’s documentation for
explanations of how to use it to drive your event loop, and when and how to use multiple
event queues in your app.

In this paradigm, your `State` needs to implement `Dispatch<O, _>` for every Wayland object `O` it needs to
process events for. This is ensured by the fact that, whenever creating an object using the methods on
an other object, you need to pass a [ QueueHandle<State>](https://docs.rs/struct.QueueHandle.html) from the

[that will be managing the newly created object.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`However, implementing all those traits on your own is a lot of (often uninteresting) work. To make this
easier a composition mechanism is provided using the [ delegate_dispatch!](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro. This way, another
library (such as Smithay’s Client Toolkit) can provide generic

[implementations that you can reuse in your own app by delegating those objects to that provided implementation. See the documentation of those traits and macro for details.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started-example)Getting started example

As an overview of how this crate is used, here is a commented example of a program that connects to the
Wayland server and lists the globals this server advertised through the `wl_registry`:

```
use wayland_client::{protocol::wl_registry, Connection, Dispatch, QueueHandle};
// This struct represents the state of our app. This simple app does not
// need any state, but this type still supports the `Dispatch` implementations.
struct AppData;
// Implement `Dispatch<WlRegistry, ()> for our state. This provides the logic
// to be able to process events for the wl_registry interface.
//
// The second type parameter is the user-data of our implementation. It is a
// mechanism that allows you to associate a value to each particular Wayland
// object, and allow different dispatching logic depending on the type of the
// associated value.
//
// In this example, we just use () as we don't have any value to associate. See
// the `Dispatch` documentation for more details about this.
impl Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, ()> for AppData {
    fn event(
        _state: &mut Self,
        _: &wl_registry::WlRegistry,
        event: wl_registry::Event,
        _: &(),
        _: &Connection,
        _: &QueueHandle<AppData>,
    ) {
        // When receiving events from the wl_registry, we are only interested in the
        // `global` event, which signals a new available global.
        // When receiving this event, we just print its characteristics in this example.
        if let wl_registry::Event::Global { name, interface, version } = event {
            println!("[{}] {} (v{})", name, interface, version);
        }
    }
}
// The main function of our program
fn main() {
    // Create a Wayland connection by connecting to the server through the
    // environment-provided configuration.
    let conn = Connection::connect_to_env().unwrap();
    // Retrieve the WlDisplay Wayland object from the connection. This object is
    // the starting point of any Wayland program, from which all other objects will
    // be created.
    let display = conn.display();
    // Create an event queue for our event processing
    let mut event_queue = conn.new_event_queue();
    // And get its handle to associate new objects to it
    let qh = event_queue.handle();
    // Create a wl_registry object by sending the wl_display.get_registry request.
    // This method takes two arguments: a handle to the queue that the newly created
    // wl_registry will be assigned to, and the user-data that should be associated
    // with this registry (here it is () as we don't need user-data).
    let _registry = display.get_registry(&qh, ());
    // At this point everything is ready, and we just need to wait to receive the events
    // from the wl_registry. Our callback will print the advertised globals.
    println!("Advertised globals:");
    // To actually receive the events, we invoke the `roundtrip` method. This method
    // is special and you will generally only invoke it during the setup of your program:
    // it will block until the server has received and processed all the messages you've
    // sent up to now.
    //
    // In our case, that means it'll block until the server has received our
    // wl_display.get_registry request, and as a reaction has sent us a batch of
    // wl_registry.global events.
    //
    // `roundtrip` will then empty the internal buffer of the queue it has been invoked
    // on, and thus invoke our `Dispatch` implementation that prints the list of advertised
    // globals.
    event_queue.roundtrip(&mut AppData).unwrap();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-use)Advanced use

It may be that for some of your objects, handling them via the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) is impractical. For example,
if processing the events from those objects doesn’t require accessing some global state, and/or you need to
handle them in a context where cranking an event loop is impractical.

In those contexts, this crate also provides some escape hatches to directly interface with the low-level
APIs from `wayland-backend`, allowing you to register callbacks for those objects that will be invoked
whenever they receive an event and *any* event queue from the program is being dispatched. Those
callbacks are more constrained: they don’t get a `&mut State` reference, and must be threadsafe. See
[ Proxy::send_constructor()](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html#tymethod.send_constructor) and

[for details about how to assign such callbacks to objects.](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-ffi)Interaction with FFI

It can happen that you’ll need to interact with Wayland states accross FFI. A typical example would be if
you need to use the [ raw-window-handle](https://docs.rs/raw-window-handle/) crate.

In this case, you’ll need enable the `system` feature to use the `libwayland` backend of
`wayland-backend`.

- If you need to send pointers to FFI, you can retrive the `*mut wl_proxy`pointers from the proxies by first getting the`ObjectId``Proxy::id()``ObjectId::as_ptr()`

# wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-client/0.31.14/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/wayland_client/

## Expand description

Interface for interacting with the Wayland protocol, client-side.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-concepts)General concepts

This crate is structured around four main objects: the [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) and

[structs, proxies (objects implementing the](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[trait), and the](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html)

`Proxy`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`The [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) is the heart of this crate. It represents your connection to the Wayland server, and
you’ll generally initialize it using the

[method, which will attempt to open a Wayland connection following the configuration specified by the ! environment.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.connect_to_env)

`Connection::connect_to_env()`Once you have a [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html), you can create an

[from it. This](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[will take care of processing events from the Wayland server and delivering them to your processing logic, in the form of a state struct with several](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[implementations (see below).](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`Each of the Wayland objects you can manipulate is represented by a struct implementing the [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html)
trait. Those structs are automatically generated from the wayland XML protocol specification. This crate
provides the types generated from the core protocol in the

[module. For other standard protocols, see the](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol``wayland-protocols` crate.[§](https://docs.rs#event-dispatching)Event dispatching

The core event dispatching logic provided by this crate is built around the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) struct. In
this paradigm, receiving and processing events is a two-step process:

- First, events are read from the Wayland socket. For each event, the backend figures out which `EventQueue`
- Then, the `EventQueue``Dispatch::event()``State`value that was provided to it.

The main goal of this structure is to make your `State` accessible without synchronization to most of
your event-processing logic, to reduce the plumbing costs. See [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)’s documentation for
explanations of how to use it to drive your event loop, and when and how to use multiple
event queues in your app.

In this paradigm, your `State` needs to implement `Dispatch<O, _>` for every Wayland object `O` it needs to
process events for. This is ensured by the fact that, whenever creating an object using the methods on
an other object, you need to pass a [ QueueHandle<State>](https://docs.rs/struct.QueueHandle.html) from the

[that will be managing the newly created object.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`However, implementing all those traits on your own is a lot of (often uninteresting) work. To make this
easier a composition mechanism is provided using the [ delegate_dispatch!](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro. This way, another
library (such as Smithay’s Client Toolkit) can provide generic

[implementations that you can reuse in your own app by delegating those objects to that provided implementation. See the documentation of those traits and macro for details.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started-example)Getting started example

As an overview of how this crate is used, here is a commented example of a program that connects to the
Wayland server and lists the globals this server advertised through the `wl_registry`:

```
use wayland_client::{protocol::wl_registry, Connection, Dispatch, QueueHandle};
// This struct represents the state of our app. This simple app does not
// need any state, but this type still supports the `Dispatch` implementations.
struct AppData;
// Implement `Dispatch<WlRegistry, ()> for our state. This provides the logic
// to be able to process events for the wl_registry interface.
//
// The second type parameter is the user-data of our implementation. It is a
// mechanism that allows you to associate a value to each particular Wayland
// object, and allow different dispatching logic depending on the type of the
// associated value.
//
// In this example, we just use () as we don't have any value to associate. See
// the `Dispatch` documentation for more details about this.
impl Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, ()> for AppData {
    fn event(
        _state: &mut Self,
        _: &wl_registry::WlRegistry,
        event: wl_registry::Event,
        _: &(),
        _: &Connection,
        _: &QueueHandle<AppData>,
    ) {
        // When receiving events from the wl_registry, we are only interested in the
        // `global` event, which signals a new available global.
        // When receiving this event, we just print its characteristics in this example.
        if let wl_registry::Event::Global { name, interface, version } = event {
            println!("[{}] {} (v{})", name, interface, version);
        }
    }
}
// The main function of our program
fn main() {
    // Create a Wayland connection by connecting to the server through the
    // environment-provided configuration.
    let conn = Connection::connect_to_env().unwrap();
    // Retrieve the WlDisplay Wayland object from the connection. This object is
    // the starting point of any Wayland program, from which all other objects will
    // be created.
    let display = conn.display();
    // Create an event queue for our event processing
    let mut event_queue = conn.new_event_queue();
    // And get its handle to associate new objects to it
    let qh = event_queue.handle();
    // Create a wl_registry object by sending the wl_display.get_registry request.
    // This method takes two arguments: a handle to the queue that the newly created
    // wl_registry will be assigned to, and the user-data that should be associated
    // with this registry (here it is () as we don't need user-data).
    let _registry = display.get_registry(&qh, ());
    // At this point everything is ready, and we just need to wait to receive the events
    // from the wl_registry. Our callback will print the advertised globals.
    println!("Advertised globals:");
    // To actually receive the events, we invoke the `roundtrip` method. This method
    // is special and you will generally only invoke it during the setup of your program:
    // it will block until the server has received and processed all the messages you've
    // sent up to now.
    //
    // In our case, that means it'll block until the server has received our
    // wl_display.get_registry request, and as a reaction has sent us a batch of
    // wl_registry.global events.
    //
    // `roundtrip` will then empty the internal buffer of the queue it has been invoked
    // on, and thus invoke our `Dispatch` implementation that prints the list of advertised
    // globals.
    event_queue.roundtrip(&mut AppData).unwrap();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-use)Advanced use

It may be that for some of your objects, handling them via the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) is impractical. For example,
if processing the events from those objects doesn’t require accessing some global state, and/or you need to
handle them in a context where cranking an event loop is impractical.

In those contexts, this crate also provides some escape hatches to directly interface with the low-level
APIs from `wayland-backend`, allowing you to register callbacks for those objects that will be invoked
whenever they receive an event and *any* event queue from the program is being dispatched. Those
callbacks are more constrained: they don’t get a `&mut State` reference, and must be threadsafe. See
[ Proxy::send_constructor()](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html#tymethod.send_constructor) and

[for details about how to assign such callbacks to objects.](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-ffi)Interaction with FFI

It can happen that you’ll need to interact with Wayland states accross FFI. A typical example would be if
you need to use the [ raw-window-handle](https://docs.rs/raw-window-handle/) crate.

In this case, you’ll need enable the `system` feature to use the `libwayland` backend of
`wayland-backend`.

- If you need to send pointers to FFI, you can retrive the `*mut wl_proxy`pointers from the proxies by first getting the`ObjectId``Proxy::id()``ObjectId::as_ptr()`

# Connection in wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-client/^0.31.14/struct.Connection.html

`pub struct Connection { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The Wayland connection

This is the main type representing your connection to the Wayland server, though most of the interaction
with the protocol are actually done using other types. The two main uses a simple app has for the
[ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) are:

- Obtaining the initial `WlDisplay``display()`
- Creating new `EventQueue``new_event_queue()`

It can be created through the [ connect_to_env()](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.connect_to_env) method to follow the
configuration from the environment (which is what you’ll do most of the time), or using the

[method if you retrieved your connected Wayland socket through other means.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.from_socket)

`from_socket()`In case you need to plug yourself into an external Wayland connection that you don’t control, you’ll
likely get access to it as a [ Backend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.Backend.html), in which case you can create a

[from it using the](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)

`Connection`[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.from_backend)

Do a roundtrip to the server

# EventQueue in wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-client/^0.31.14/struct.EventQueue.html

`pub struct EventQueue<State> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An event queue

This is an abstraction for handling event dispatching, that allows you to ensure
access to some common state `&mut State` to your event handlers.

Event queues are created through [ Connection::new_event_queue()](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.new_event_queue).

Upon creation, a wayland object is assigned to an event queue by passing the associated [ QueueHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.QueueHandle.html)
as argument to the method creating it. All events received by that object will be processed by that event
queue, when

[or](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.dispatch_pending)

`dispatch_pending()`[is invoked.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.blocking_dispatch)

`blocking_dispatch()`[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#single-queue-app)Single queue app

If your app is simple enough that the only source of event to process is the Wayland socket and you only need a single event queue, your main loop can be as simple as this:

```
use wayland_client::Connection;
let connection = Connection::connect_to_env().unwrap();
let mut event_queue = connection.new_event_queue();
/*
 * Here your initial setup
 */
// And the main loop:
while !state.exit {
    event_queue.blocking_dispatch(&mut state).unwrap();
}
```
The [ blocking_dispatch()](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.blocking_dispatch) call will wait (by putting the thread to sleep)
until there are some events from the server that can be processed, and all your actual app logic can be
done in the callbacks of the

[implementations, and in the main](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch``loop` after the
[call.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.blocking_dispatch)

`blocking_dispatch()`[§](https://docs.rs#multi-thread-multi-queue-app)Multi-thread multi-queue app

In a case where you app is multithreaded and you want to process events in multiple thread, a simple
pattern is to have one [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) per thread processing Wayland events.

With this pattern, each thread can use [ EventQueue::blocking_dispatch()](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.blocking_dispatch)
on its own event loop, and everything will “Just Work”.

[§](https://docs.rs#single-queue-guest-library)Single-queue guest library

If your code is some library code that will act on a Wayland connection shared by the main program, it is
likely you should not trigger socket reads yourself and instead let the main app take care of it. In this
case, to ensure your [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) still makes progress, you should regularly invoke

[which will process the events that were enqueued in the inner buffer of your](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.dispatch_pending)

`EventQueue::dispatch_pending()`[by the main app reading the socket.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[§](https://docs.rs#integrating-the-event-queue-with-other-sources-of-events)Integrating the event queue with other sources of events

If your program needs to monitor other sources of events alongside the Wayland socket using a monitoring
system like `epoll`, you can integrate the Wayland socket into this system. This is done with the help
of the [ EventQueue::prepare_read()](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.prepare_read) method. You event loop will be a bit more
explicit:

```
loop {
    // flush the outgoing buffers to ensure that the server does receive the messages
    // you've sent
    event_queue.flush().unwrap();
    // (this step is only relevant if other threads might be reading the socket as well)
    // make sure you don't have any pending events if the event queue that might have been
    // enqueued by other threads reading the socket
    event_queue.dispatch_pending(&mut state).unwrap();
    // This puts in place some internal synchronization to prepare for the fact that
    // you're going to wait for events on the socket and read them, in case other threads
    // are doing the same thing
    let read_guard = event_queue.prepare_read().unwrap();
    /*
     * At this point you can invoke epoll(..) to wait for readiness on the multiple FD you
     * are working with, and read_guard.connection_fd() will give you the FD to wait on for
     * the Wayland connection
     */
    if wayland_socket_ready {
        // If epoll notified readiness of the Wayland socket, you can now proceed to the read
        read_guard.read().unwrap();
        // And now, you must invoke dispatch_pending() to actually process the events
        event_queue.dispatch_pending(&mut state).unwrap();
    } else {
        // otherwise, some of your other FD are ready, but you didn't receive Wayland events,
        // you can drop the guard to cancel the read preparation
        std::mem::drop(read_guard);
    }
    /*
     * There you process all relevant events from your other event sources
     */
}
```

Dispatch pending events

Events are accumulated in the event queue internal buffer when the Wayland socket is read using
the read APIs on [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html), or when reading is done from an other thread.
This method will dispatch all such pending events by sequentially invoking their associated handlers:
the

[implementations on the provided](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch``&mut D`.Note: this may block if another thread has frozen the queue.

Synchronous roundtrip

This function will cause a synchronous round trip with the wayland server. This function will block until all requests in the queue are sent and processed by the server.

This function may be useful during initial setup of your app. This function may also be useful where you need to guarantee all requests prior to calling this function are completed.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_client/event_queue.rs.html#545-568)

#### pub fn [poll_dispatch_pending](https://docs.rs#method.poll_dispatch_pending)(
    &mut self,
    cx: &mut [Context](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/task/wake/struct.Context.html)<'_>,
    data: [&mut State](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [Poll](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/task/poll/enum.Poll.html)<[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Infallible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/enum.Infallible.html), [DispatchError](https://docs.rs/enum.DispatchError.html)>>

Attempt to dispatch events from this queue, registering the current task for wakeup if no events are pending.

This method is similar to [ dispatch_pending()](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html#method.dispatch_pending); it will not
perform reads on the Wayland socket.  Reads on the socket by other tasks or threads will
cause the current task to wake up if events are pending on this queue.

```
use futures_channel::mpsc::Receiver;
use futures_util::future::{poll_fn,select};
use futures_util::stream::StreamExt;
use wayland_client::EventQueue;
struct Data;
enum AppEvent {
    SomethingHappened(u32),
}
impl Data {
    fn handle(&mut self, event: AppEvent) {
        // actual event handling goes here
    }
}
// An async task that is spawned on an executor in order to handle events that need access
// to a specific data object.
async fn run(data: &mut Data, mut wl_queue: EventQueue<Data>, mut app_queue: Receiver<AppEvent>)
    -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>
{
    use futures_util::future::Either;
    loop {
        match select(
            poll_fn(|cx| wl_queue.poll_dispatch_pending(cx, data)),
            app_queue.next(),
        ).await {
            Either::Left((res, _)) => match res? {},
            Either::Right((Some(event), _)) => {
                data.handle(event);
            }
            Either::Right((None, _)) => return Ok(()),
        }
    }
}
```

}## Expand description

A trait for handlers of proxies’ events delivered to an [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#general-usage)General usage

You need to implement this trait on your `State` for every type of Wayland object that will be processed
by the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) working with your

`State`.You can have different implementations of the trait for the same interface but different `UserData` type.
This way the events for a given object will be processed by the adequate implementation depending on
which `UserData` was assigned to it at creation.

The way this trait works is that the [ Dispatch::event()](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html#tymethod.event) method will be invoked by the event queue for
every event received by an object associated to this event queue. Your implementation can then match on
the associated

[enum and do any processing needed with that event.](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html#associatedtype.Event)

`Proxy::Event`In the rare case of an interface with *events* creating new objects (in the core protocol, the only
instance of this is the `wl_data_device.data_offer` event), you’ll need to implement the
[ Dispatch::event_created_child()](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html#method.event_created_child) method. See the

[macro for a simple way to do this.](https://docs.rs/macro.event_created_child.html)

`event_created_child!()`[§](https://docs.rs#modularity)Modularity

To provide generic handlers for downstream usage, it is possible to make an implementation of the trait
that is generic over the last type argument, as illustrated below. Users will then be able to
automatically delegate their implementation to yours using the [ delegate_dispatch!()](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro.

As a result, when your implementation is instantiated, the last type parameter `State` will be the state
struct of the app using your generic implementation. You can put additional trait constraints on it to
specify an interface between your module and downstream code, as illustrated in this example:

```
use wayland_client::{protocol::wl_registry, Dispatch};
/// The type we want to delegate to
struct DelegateToMe;
/// The user data relevant for your implementation.
/// When providing a delegate implementation, it is recommended to use your own type here, even if it is
/// just a unit struct: using () would cause a risk of clashing with another such implementation.
struct MyUserData;
// Now a generic implementation of Dispatch, we are generic over the last type argument instead of using
// the default State=Self.
impl<State> Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, MyUserData, State> for DelegateToMe
where
    // State is the type which has delegated to this type, so it needs to have an impl of Dispatch itself
    State: Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, MyUserData>,
    // If your delegate type has some internal state, it'll need to access it, and you can
    // require it by adding custom trait bounds.
    // In this example, we just require an AsMut implementation
    State: AsMut<DelegateToMe>,
{
    fn event(
        state: &mut State,
        _proxy: &wl_registry::WlRegistry,
        _event: wl_registry::Event,
        _udata: &MyUserData,
        _conn: &wayland_client::Connection,
        _qhandle: &wayland_client::QueueHandle<State>,
    ) {
        // Here the delegate may handle incoming events as it pleases.
        // For example, it retrives its state and does some processing with it
        let me: &mut DelegateToMe = state.as_mut();
        // do something with `me` ...
    }
}
```
**Note:** Due to limitations in Rust’s trait resolution algorithm, a type providing a generic
implementation of [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) cannot be used directly as the dispatching state, as rustc
currently fails to understand that it also provides

`Dispatch<I, U, Self>` (assuming all other
trait bounds are respected as well).## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

# delegate_dispatch in wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-client/^0.31.14/macro.delegate_dispatch.html

```
macro_rules! delegate_dispatch {
    ($(@< $( $lt:tt $( : $clt:tt $(+ $dlt:tt )* )? ),+ >)? $dispatch_from:ty : [$interface: ty: $udata: ty] => $dispatch_to: ty) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A helper macro which delegates a set of [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) implementations for proxies to some other type which
provides a generic

[implementation.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`This macro allows more easily delegating smaller parts of the protocol an application may wish to handle in a modular fashion.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

For example, say you want to delegate events for [ WlRegistry](https://docs.rs/protocol/wl_registry/struct.WlRegistry.html)
to the struct

`DelegateToMe` for the [documentation example.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch````
use wayland_client::{delegate_dispatch, protocol::wl_registry};
// ExampleApp is the type events will be dispatched to.
/// The application state
struct ExampleApp {
    /// The delegate for handling wl_registry events.
    delegate: DelegateToMe,
}
// Use delegate_dispatch to implement Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, MyUserData> for ExampleApp
delegate_dispatch!(ExampleApp: [wl_registry::WlRegistry: MyUserData] => DelegateToMe);
// DelegateToMe requires that ExampleApp implements AsMut<DelegateToMe>, so we provide the
// trait implementation.
impl AsMut<DelegateToMe> for ExampleApp {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut DelegateToMe {
        &mut self.delegate
    }
}
// To explain the macro above, you may read it as the following:
//
// For ExampleApp, delegate WlRegistry to DelegateToMe.
// Assert ExampleApp can Dispatch events for wl_registry
fn assert_is_registry_delegate<T>()
where
    T: Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, MyUserData>,
{
}
assert_is_registry_delegate::<ExampleApp>();
// This macro can also be applied to a generic type using the `@<>` syntax:
/// The application state
struct GenericApp<T: Copy> {
    /// The delegate for handling wl_registry events.
    delegate: DelegateToMe,
    app_data: T,
}
delegate_dispatch!(@<T: Copy> GenericApp<T>: [wl_registry::WlRegistry: MyUserData] => DelegateToMe);
impl<T: Copy> AsMut<DelegateToMe> for GenericApp<T> {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut DelegateToMe {
        &mut self.delegate
    }
}
// Assert that the above setup applies to a concrete GenericApp type
assert_is_registry_delegate::<GenericApp<u32>>();
```

# raw_window_handle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/raw-window-handle/

## Expand description

Interoperability library for Rust Windowing applications.

This library provides standard types for accessing a window’s platform-specific raw window handle and platforms display handle. This does not provide any utilities for creating and managing windows; instead, it provides a common interface that window creation libraries (e.g. Winit, SDL) can use to easily talk with graphics libraries (e.g. gfx-hal).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-guarantees)Safety guarantees

Please see the docs of [ HasWindowHandle](https://docs.rs/trait.HasWindowHandle.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.HasDisplayHandle.html)

`HasDisplayHandle`[§](https://docs.rs#platform-handle-initialization)Platform handle initialization

Each platform handle struct is purposefully non-exhaustive, so that additional fields may be
added without breaking backwards compatibility. Each struct provides an `empty` method that may
be used along with the struct update syntax to construct it. See each specific struct for
examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#display-handles)Display Handles

Some windowing systems use a separate display handle for some operations. The display usually
represents a connection to some display server, but it is not necessarily tied to a particular
window. See [ RawDisplayHandle](https://docs.rs/enum.RawDisplayHandle.html) for more details.

# delegate_noop in wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-client/^0.31.14/macro.delegate_noop.html

```
macro_rules! delegate_noop {
    ($(@< $( $lt:tt $( : $clt:tt $(+ $dlt:tt )* )? ),+ >)? $dispatch_from: ty : $interface: ty) => { ... };
    ($(@< $( $lt:tt $( : $clt:tt $(+ $dlt:tt )* )? ),+ >)? $dispatch_from: ty : ignore $interface: ty) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A helper macro which delegates a set of [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) implementations for proxies to a static handler.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This macro is useful to implement [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) for interfaces where events are unimportant to
the current application and can be ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_client::{delegate_noop, protocol::{wl_data_offer, wl_subcompositor}};
/// The application state
struct ExampleApp {
    // ...
}
// Ignore all events for this interface:
delegate_noop!(ExampleApp: ignore wl_data_offer::WlDataOffer);
// This interface should not emit events:
delegate_noop!(ExampleApp: wl_subcompositor::WlSubcompositor);
```
This last example will execute `unreachable!()` if the interface emits any events.

---

# event_created_child in wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-client/^0.31.14/macro.event_created_child.html

```
macro_rules! event_created_child {
    ($(@< $( $lt:tt $( : $clt:tt $(+ $dlt:tt )* )? ),+ >)? $selftype:ty, $iface:ty, [$($opcode:pat => ($child_iface:ty, $child_udata:expr)),* $(,)?]) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Macro used to override `Dispatch::event_created_child()`

Use this macro inside the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) implementation to override this method, to implement the
initialization of the user data for event-created objects. The usage syntax is as follow:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl Dispatch<WlFoo, FooUserData> for MyState {
    fn event(
        &mut self,
        proxy: &WlFoo,
        event: FooEvent,
        data: &FooUserData,
        connhandle: &mut ConnectionHandle,
        qhandle: &QueueHandle<MyState>
    ) {
        /* ... */
    }
    event_created_child!(MyState, WlFoo, [
    // there can be multiple lines if this interface has multiple object-creating event
        EVT_CREATE_BAR => (WlBar, BarUserData::new()),
    //  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~     ~~~~~  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    //    |                  |      |
    //    |                  |      +-- an expression whose evaluation produces the
    //    |                  |          user data value
    //    |                  +-- the type of the newly created object
    //    +-- the opcode of the event that creates a new object, constants for those are
    //        generated alongside the `WlFoo` type in the `wl_foo` module
    ]);
}
```

### impl [CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)

Search for a theme with the given name in the given search paths, and returns an XCursorTheme which represents it. If no inheritance can be determined, then the themes inherits from the “default” theme.

Try to load an icon from the theme. If the icon is not found within this theme’s directories, then the function looks at the theme from which this theme is inherited.

Try to load an icon from the theme, returning it with its inheritance depth.

If the icon is not found within this theme’s directories, then the function looks at the theme from which this theme is inherited. The second element of the returned tuple indicates how many levels of inheritance were traversed before the icon was found.

# wayland_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-cursor/0.31.14/aarch64-apple-darwin/wayland_cursor/

## Expand description

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to re-implement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a [ CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html), which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the [ get_cursor()](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.get_cursor) method, you can load a
specific

[, which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to attach them to a wayland surface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
// Load the default cursor theme.
let mut cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(&connection, shm, 32)
    .expect("Could not load cursor theme");
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait")
    .expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
    // Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
    let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
    let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
    // Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
    let buffer = &cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
    // and attach it to a wl_surface.
    cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
    cursor_surface.commit();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(fr_info.frame_duration as u64));
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)
- A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorImageBuffer.html)- Image - Buffer
- A buffer containing a cursor image.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)- Theme
- Represents a cursor theme loaded from the system.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameAndDuration.html)- AndDuration
- Which frame to show, and for how long.

[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// # use wayland_client::{Connection, backend::InvalidId, protocol::wl_shm};
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    /// # fn example(conn: &Connection, shm: wl_shm::WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<CursorTheme, InvalidId> {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// CursorTheme::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    /// # }
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// ```
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    pub fn load(conn: &Connection, shm: WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)        Self::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    }
[122](https://docs.rs#122)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// Load a cursor theme, using `name` as fallback.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    ///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// The theme name and cursor size are read from the `XCURSOR_THEME` and
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// `XCURSOR_SIZE` environment variables, respectively, or from the provided variables
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// if those are invalid.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    pub fn load_or(
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        conn: &Connection,
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        shm: WlShm,
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        name: &str,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)        mut size: u32,
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    ) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        let name_string = String::from(name);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)        let name = &env::var("XCURSOR_THEME").unwrap_or(name_string);
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        if let Ok(var) = env::var("XCURSOR_SIZE") {
[138](https://docs.rs#138)            if let Ok(int) = var.parse() {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)                size = int;
[140](https://docs.rs#140)            }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)        Self::load_from_name(conn, shm, name, size)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    }
[145](https://docs.rs#145)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// Create a new cursor theme, ignoring the system defaults.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    pub fn load_from_name(
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        conn: &Connection,
[149](https://docs.rs#149)        shm: WlShm,
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        name: &str,
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        size: u32,
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    ) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> {
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        // Set some minimal cursor size to hold it. We're not using `size` argument for that,
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        // because the actual size that we'll use depends on theme sizes available on a system.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        // The minimal size covers most common minimal theme size, which is 16.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        const INITIAL_POOL_SIZE: i32 = 16 * 16 * 4;
[157](https://docs.rs#157)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        //  Create shm.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        let mem_fd = create_shm_fd().expect("Shm fd allocation failed");
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        let mut file = File::from(mem_fd);
[161](https://docs.rs#161)        file.set_len(INITIAL_POOL_SIZE as u64).expect("Failed to set buffer length");
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        // Ensure that we have the same we requested.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        file.write_all(&[0; INITIAL_POOL_SIZE as usize]).expect("Write to shm fd failed");
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        // Flush to ensure the compositor has access to the buffer when it tries to map it.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        file.flush().expect("Flush on shm fd failed");
[167](https://docs.rs#167)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)        let pool_id = conn.send_request(
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            &shm,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)            wl_shm::Request::CreatePool { fd: file.as_fd(), size: INITIAL_POOL_SIZE },
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            Some(Arc::new(IgnoreObjectData)),
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        )?;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        let pool = WlShmPool::from_id(conn, pool_id)?;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        let name = String::from(name);
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        Ok(Self {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            name,
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            file,
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            size,
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            pool,
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            pool_size: INITIAL_POOL_SIZE,
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            cursors: Vec::new(),
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            backend: conn.backend().downgrade(),
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            fallback: None,
[186](https://docs.rs#186)        })
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    /// Retrieve a cursor from the theme.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// This method returns [`None`] if this cursor is not provided either by the theme, or by one of its parents.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    ///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// If a [fallback is set], it will use the data returned by the fallback.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    ///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// [fallback is set]: Self::set_fallback()
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    pub fn get_cursor(&mut self, name: &str) -> Option<&Cursor> {
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        match self.cursors.iter().position(|cursor| cursor.name == name) {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)            Some(i) => Some(&self.cursors[i]),
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            None => {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)                let cursor = match self.load_cursor(name, self.size) {
[201](https://docs.rs#201)                    None => {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)                        let fallback = self.fallback.as_ref()?;
[203](https://docs.rs#203)                        let data = fallback.0(name, self.size)?;
[204](https://docs.rs#204)                        let images = xparser::parse_xcursor(&data)?;
[205](https://docs.rs#205)                        let conn = Connection::from_backend(self.backend.upgrade()?);
[206](https://docs.rs#206)                        Cursor::new(&conn, name, self, &images, self.size)
[207](https://docs.rs#207)                    }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)                    Some(cursor) => cursor,
[209](https://docs.rs#209)                };
[210](https://docs.rs#210)                self.cursors.push(cursor);
[211](https://docs.rs#211)                self.cursors.iter().last()
[212](https://docs.rs#212)            }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// Set a fallback to load the cursor data, in case the system theme is missing a cursor that you need.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    ///
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// Your fallback will be invoked with the name and size of the requested cursor and should return a byte
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// array with the contents of an `xcursor` file, or [`None`] if you don't provide a fallback for this cursor.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// For example, this defines a generic fallback cursor image and uses it for all missing cursors:
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    /// ```ignore
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// use wayland_client::{Connection, backend::InvalidId, protocol::wl_shm};
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// fn example(conn: &Connection, shm: wl_shm::WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<CursorTheme, InvalidId> {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    ///   let mut theme = CursorTheme::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)?;
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    ///   theme.set_fallback(|name, size| {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    ///       include_bytes!("./icons/default")
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///   });
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    ///   Ok(theme)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// ```
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    pub fn set_fallback<F>(&mut self, fallback: F)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    where
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        F: Fn(&str, u32) -> Option<Cow<'static, [u8]>> + Send + Sync + 'static,
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        self.fallback = Some(FallBack::new(fallback))
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// This function loads a cursor, parses it and pushes the images onto the shm pool.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    ///
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// Keep in mind that if the cursor is already loaded, the function will make a duplicate.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    fn load_cursor(&mut self, name: &str, size: u32) -> Option<Cursor> {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        let conn = Connection::from_backend(self.backend.upgrade()?);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        let icon_path = XCursorTheme::load(&self.name).load_icon(name)?;
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        let mut icon_file = File::open(icon_path).ok()?;
[247](https://docs.rs#247)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let mut buf = Vec::new();
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        let images = {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            icon_file.read_to_end(&mut buf).ok()?;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)            xparser::parse_xcursor(&buf)?
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        };
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        Some(Cursor::new(&conn, name, self, &images, size))
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    }
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// Grow the wl_shm_pool this theme is stored on.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// This method does nothing if the provided size is smaller or equal to the pool's current size.
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    fn grow(&mut self, size: i32) {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        if size > self.pool_size {
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            self.file.set_len(size as u64).expect("Failed to set new buffer length");
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            self.pool.resize(size);
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            self.pool_size = size;
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    }

[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[271](https://docs.rs#271)pub struct Cursor {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    name: String,
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    images: Vec<CursorImageBuffer>,
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    total_duration: u32,
[275](https://docs.rs#275)}
[276](https://docs.rs#276)
[277](https://docs.rs#277)impl Cursor {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// Construct a new Cursor.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    /// Each of the provided images will be written into `theme`.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// This will also grow `theme.pool` if necessary.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    fn new(
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        conn: &Connection,
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        name: &str,
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        theme: &mut CursorTheme,
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        images: &[XCursorImage],
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        size: u32,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    ) -> Self {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)        let mut total_duration = 0;
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        let images: Vec<CursorImageBuffer> = Self::nearest_images(size, images)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            .map(|image| {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)                let buffer = CursorImageBuffer::new(conn, theme, image);
[293](https://docs.rs#293)                total_duration += buffer.delay;
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)                buffer
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            })
[297](https://docs.rs#297)            .collect();
[298](https://docs.rs#298)
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        Self { total_duration, name: String::from(name), images }
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    fn nearest_images(size: u32, images: &[XCursorImage]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &XCursorImage> {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        // Follow the nominal size of the cursor to choose the nearest
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        let nearest_image =
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            images.iter().min_by_key(|image| (size as i32 - image.size as i32).abs()).unwrap();
[306](https://docs.rs#306)
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        images.iter().filter(move |image| {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            image.width == nearest_image.width && image.height == nearest_image.height
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        })
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    }
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// Given a time, calculate which frame to show, and how much time remains until the next frame.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    ///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// Time will wrap, so if for instance the cursor has an animation lasting 100ms,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// then calling this function with 5ms and 105ms as input gives the same output.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    pub fn frame_and_duration(&self, mut millis: u32) -> FrameAndDuration {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        millis %= self.total_duration;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        let mut res = 0;
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        for (i, img) in self.images.iter().enumerate() {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            if millis < img.delay {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                res = i;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                break;
[324](https://docs.rs#324)            }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            millis -= img.delay;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        }
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        FrameAndDuration { frame_index: res, frame_duration: millis }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    }
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    /// Total number of images forming this cursor animation
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    pub fn image_count(&self) -> usize {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        self.images.len()
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    }

[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// A buffer containing a cursor image.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// You can access the `WlBuffer` via `Deref`.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// Note that this buffer is internally managed by wayland-cursor, as such you should
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// not try to act on it beyond assigning it to `wl_surface`s.
[351](https://docs.rs#351)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[352](https://docs.rs#352)pub struct CursorImageBuffer {
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    buffer: WlBuffer,
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    delay: u32,
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    xhot: u32,
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    yhot: u32,
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    width: u32,
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    height: u32,
[359](https://docs.rs#359)}
[360](https://docs.rs#360)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)impl CursorImageBuffer {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// Construct a new CursorImageBuffer
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    ///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// This function appends the pixels of the image to the provided file,
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// and constructs a wl_buffer on that data.
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    fn new(conn: &Connection, theme: &mut CursorTheme, image: &XCursorImage) -> Self {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        let buf = &image.pixels_rgba;
[368](https://docs.rs#368)        let offset = theme.file.seek(SeekFrom::End(0)).unwrap();
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        // Resize memory before writing to it to handle shm correctly.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        let new_size = offset + buf.len() as u64;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        theme.grow(new_size as i32);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        theme.file.write_all(buf).unwrap();
[375](https://docs.rs#375)
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        let buffer_id = conn
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            .send_request(
[378](https://docs.rs#378)                &theme.pool,
[379](https://docs.rs#379)                wl_shm_pool::Request::CreateBuffer {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)                    offset: offset as i32,
[381](https://docs.rs#381)                    width: image.width as i32,
[382](https://docs.rs#382)                    height: image.height as i32,
[383](https://docs.rs#383)                    stride: (image.width * 4) as i32,
[384](https://docs.rs#384)                    format: WEnum::Value(Format::Argb8888),
[385](https://docs.rs#385)                },
[386](https://docs.rs#386)                Some(Arc::new(IgnoreObjectData)),
[387](https://docs.rs#387)            )
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            .unwrap();
[389](https://docs.rs#389)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        let buffer = WlBuffer::from_id(conn, buffer_id).unwrap();
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        Self {
[393](https://docs.rs#393)            buffer,
[394](https://docs.rs#394)            delay: image.delay,
[395](https://docs.rs#395)            xhot: image.xhot,
[396](https://docs.rs#396)            yhot: image.yhot,
[397](https://docs.rs#397)            width: image.width,
[398](https://docs.rs#398)            height: image.height,
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    }

[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// Which frame to show, and for how long.

[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// Create a shared file descriptor in memory.
[438](https://docs.rs#438)fn create_shm_fd() -> IoResult<OwnedFd> {
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    // Only try memfd on systems that provide it, (like Linux, Android)
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    #[cfg(any(target_os = "linux", target_os = "android"))]
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    loop {
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        match memfd_create(
[443](https://docs.rs#443)            CStr::from_bytes_with_nul(b"wayland-cursor-rs\0").unwrap(),
[444](https://docs.rs#444)            MemfdFlags::CLOEXEC,
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        ) {
[446](https://docs.rs#446)            Ok(fd) => return Ok(fd),
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            Err(Errno::INTR) => continue,
[448](https://docs.rs#448)            Err(Errno::NOSYS) => break,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)            Err(errno) => return Err(errno.into()),
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        }
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    }
[452](https://docs.rs#452)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    // Fallback to using shm_open.
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    let sys_time = SystemTime::now();
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    let mut mem_file_handle = format!(
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        "/wayland-cursor-rs-{}",
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        sys_time.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().subsec_nanos()
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    );
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    loop {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        match shm::open(
[461](https://docs.rs#461)            mem_file_handle.as_str(),
[462](https://docs.rs#462)            shm::OFlags::CREATE | shm::OFlags::EXCL | shm::OFlags::RDWR,
[463](https://docs.rs#463)            Mode::RUSR | Mode::WUSR,
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        ) {
[465](https://docs.rs#465)            Ok(fd) => match shm::unlink(mem_file_handle.as_str()) {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)                Ok(_) => return Ok(fd),
[467](https://docs.rs#467)                Err(errno) => return Err(IoError::from(errno)),
[468](https://docs.rs#468)            },
[469](https://docs.rs#469)            Err(Errno::EXIST) => {
[470](https://docs.rs#470)                // If a file with that handle exists then change the handle
[471](https://docs.rs#471)                mem_file_handle = format!(
[472](https://docs.rs#472)                    "/wayland-cursor-rs-{}",
[473](https://docs.rs#473)                    sys_time.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().subsec_nanos()
[474](https://docs.rs#474)                );
[475](https://docs.rs#475)                continue;
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            }

Retrieve a cursor from the theme.

This method returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if this cursor is not provided either by the theme, or by one of its parents.

If a [fallback is set](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.set_fallback), it will use the data returned by the fallback.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_cursor/lib.rs.html#233-238)#### pub fn [set_fallback](https://docs.rs#method.set_fallback)<F>(&mut self, fallback: F)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wayland_cursor/lib.rs.html#233-238)

#### pub fn [set_fallback](https://docs.rs#method.set_fallback)<F>(&mut self, fallback: F)

Set a fallback to load the cursor data, in case the system theme is missing a cursor that you need.

Your fallback will be invoked with the name and size of the requested cursor and should return a byte
array with the contents of an `xcursor` file, or [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if you don’t provide a fallback for this cursor.

For example, this defines a generic fallback cursor image and uses it for all missing cursors:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
use wayland_client::{Connection, backend::InvalidId, protocol::wl_shm};
fn example(conn: &Connection, shm: wl_shm::WlShm, size: u32) -> Result<CursorTheme, InvalidId> {
  let mut theme = CursorTheme::load_or(conn, shm, "default", size)?;
  theme.set_fallback(|name, size| {
      include_bytes!("./icons/default")
  });
  Ok(theme)
}
```

Given a time, calculate which frame to show, and how much time remains until the next frame.

Time will wrap, so if for instance the cursor has an animation lasting 100ms, then calling this function with 5ms and 105ms as input gives the same output.

# wayland_cursor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-cursor/0.31.14/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/wayland_cursor/

## Expand description

Wayland cursor utilities

This crate aims to re-implement the functionality of the `libwayland-cursor` library in Rust.

It allows you to load cursors from the system and display them correctly.

First of all, you need to create a [ CursorTheme](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html), which represents the full cursor theme.

From this theme, using the [ get_cursor()](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html#method.get_cursor) method, you can load a
specific

[, which can contain several images if the cursor is animated. It also provides you with the means of querying which frame of the animation should be displayed at what time, as well as handles to the buffers containing these frames, to attach them to a wayland surface.](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)

`Cursor`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wayland_cursor::CursorTheme;
// Load the default cursor theme.
let mut cursor_theme = CursorTheme::load(&connection, shm, 32)
    .expect("Could not load cursor theme");
let cursor = cursor_theme.get_cursor("wait")
    .expect("Cursor not provided by theme");
let start_time = Instant::now();
loop {
    // Obtain which frame we should show, and for how long.
    let millis = start_time.elapsed().as_millis();
    let fr_info = cursor.frame_and_duration(millis as u32);
    // Here, we obtain the right cursor frame...
    let buffer = &cursor[fr_info.frame_index];
    // and attach it to a wl_surface.
    cursor_surface.attach(Some(&buffer), 0, 0);
    cursor_surface.commit();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(fr_info.frame_duration as u64));
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)
- A cursor from a theme. Can contain several images if animated.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorImageBuffer.html)- Image - Buffer
- A buffer containing a cursor image.
- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.CursorTheme.html)- Theme
- Represents a cursor theme loaded from the system.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameAndDuration.html)- AndDuration
- Which frame to show, and for how long.
